opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that's one of the more interesting gray areas right now. When people say "RL," they usually picture updating the weights of the model itself, the classic policy-gradient picture. But if you're working with a closed model, you can't touch the weights, so what you're actually optimizing is everything around it: the prompts, the tool definitions, how context gets managed, when you retry, how you decompose the task, what memory you carry between steps.

I'd call that reinforcement learning in the broader sense, just over a different parameter space. You still have an environment, you still have rollouts, you still have a reward signal, and you're still searching for a policy that does better on that reward. The policy just happens to be "frozen model plus harness," and the only part that moves is the harness. Some people call it prompt optimization or program search, and that's fair. Mechanically it often looks more like evolutionary search or Bayesian optimization than gradient descent, because the parameters are discrete and you can't backprop through an API.

The useful way to think about it is as a spectrum. On one end you're tuning a few strings in a system prompt. On the other you're doing full weight updates on an open model. In between you have things like learned routing, learned retrieval, or a small trainable model sitting next to a big frozen one. They all live under the same umbrella: you define the environment and the reward, and then ask which knobs you're allowed to turn.

Practically, I think harness optimization is underrated. A lot of the gains people attribute to model improvements actually come from better scaffolding. The ceiling is lower than with weight updates, though, because you can't teach the model new skills, only how to use the ones it has more effectively. So my rule of thumb is that it's real RL, it's often the highest-leverage first step, and once you hit diminishing returns, that's your signal that you need control over the weights.

r001.rationale: The response says harness optimization is sometimes called “prompt optimization” and that this classification is fair.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a question I get a lot, and I think the honest answer is that it's a bit of a gray area, but I'd lean toward calling it RL in the broad sense while being careful about what's actually being learned.

If you take the textbook definition, reinforcement learning is about an agent interacting with an environment, getting reward signals, and updating some policy to do better over time. When the model itself is frozen behind an API, you're obviously not updating the weights. But the harness around it, the prompts, the tool scaffolding, the memory, the retry logic, the routing between sub-agents, all of that is effectively part of the policy from the environment's point of view. If you're optimizing those components against a reward, whether that's with evolutionary search, bandit-style selection over prompts, or even just a human doing a structured loop of try, measure, adjust, you're doing something that structurally looks like policy optimization. It's just that the parameters live in text and code rather than in a weight matrix.

Where I'd draw the distinction is in what gets generalized. When you do real RL on the weights, the model internalizes the behavior and you get transfer to situations you didn't explicitly tune for. When you optimize the harness, you're mostly getting a very good configuration for a particular distribution of tasks, and it tends to be brittle. The improvements don't compound the same way. So I'd say it's RL at the system level, but it's closer to hyperparameter search or program synthesis than to what people usually mean when they say they trained a model with RL.

The other thing I'd flag is that this is becoming the main lever a lot of teams actually have. Most people aren't going to fine-tune a frontier model. So the interesting research question isn't whether to call it RL, it's how much headroom there really is in the harness alone, and where you hit a wall that only the base model can get you past. My intuition is that the headroom is bigger than people think for narrow, well-specified tasks, and smaller than people hope for anything open-ended.

r001.rationale: The response describes harness optimization as system-level RL, closer to hyperparameter search or program synthesis. It mentions selecting prompts as one possible method, but does not classify the overall approach as prompt optimization.

astra-6.text: I’d classify that as system-level learning rather than model-level learning. If the model is closed and its weights aren’t changing, then whatever you’re optimizing lives in the harness: how you construct prompts, select tools, manage memory, or decide when to stop. You can still do reinforcement learning there, provided you’re actually updating a policy based on reward. The closed model is a component of that policy. But if you’re just trying a few prompts and picking the best one, I’d call that search or optimization rather than necessarily RL. The key question is: what’s learning, and what actions does it control?

r001.rationale: The candidate classifies it as system-level learning in the harness and says prompt construction may be optimized; it does not classify the reinforcement learning itself as prompt optimization.

sol-6.1.text: I’d classify it by what’s actually being optimized. If the model is closed and its weights stay fixed, but you’re using rewards to train a controller that decides what to put in context, which tools to call, or when to retry, then that controller is learning a policy. That’s reinforcement learning at the harness level. If you’re just trying prompts and keeping whichever one works best, I’d usually call that search or optimization. The important distinction is where the learning happens, rather than whether the underlying model is open or closed.

r001.rationale: The response classifies reward-trained harness controllers as reinforcement learning at the harness level. It calls trying prompts and keeping the best one search or optimization, not RL applied to the harness.
